question: Tell me about a time you had to understand work outside your function to deliver. What did you miss at first?
competency: Deliver as One Arm (cross-functional collaboration and delivery)

raiseTranscript.text: I was on the backend team and we had a tight deadline for a new reporting feature. Marketing needed different data cuts that weren't in our original spec.

I assumed their request was just a UI tweak. After talking to their analyst I realized they needed a new aggregation job that touched compliance data. I had to learn their tagging process and the legal review steps.
What changed after you understood that?
I added a two-day buffer for legal review and paired with their analyst on the query. We shipped on time and the report was used in the quarterly deck.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to understand work outside your function to deliver. What did you miss at first?
Role: backend engineer on reporting feature
Situation: marketing needed different data cuts
Actions: learned compliance tagging and legal review steps after initial assumption it was UI only
Outcome: added buffer, paired with analyst, shipped on time
Quote: "I assumed their request was just a UI tweak"
Follow-up: What changed after you understood that? - added two-day buffer and paired on query
junior.raiseFeedback: The story shows the candidate initially scoped the request too narrowly to their own function. After the follow-up they described learning the compliance process and adjusting their plan. This meets the bar for junior because they owned the gap in their understanding and delivered without escalation. The concrete detail about the legal review buffer ties the learning directly to the outcome.

lowerTranscript.text: I had to work with the frontend team on a dashboard. They kept asking for different endpoints so I just built what they asked.
What did you miss at first?
I didn't realize they needed the data in a specific format for their charts. Once they told me I updated the API.
How did that affect the timeline?
We slipped by a week but it was fine because they were behind too.

junior.lowerFeedback: The candidate treated the request as a simple handoff and only adjusted after the other team flagged the issue. The slip is explained away rather than owned. For a junior role this lowers the bar because there is no evidence of seeking to understand the other function's constraints before execution.

raiseTranscript.text: Our payments service needed a new fraud rule. The fraud team had a model but it required features from the risk platform that lived in another org.
What did you miss at first?
I assumed we could just call their existing API. After two weeks the risk team explained their SLA and data freshness constraints.
I set up a weekly sync, mapped the data latency requirements, and negotiated a lightweight batch export. We launched the rule two weeks later than planned but with no production incidents.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to understand work outside your function to deliver. What did you miss at first?

Situation: fraud rule needed risk platform features
Actions: moved from API assumption to weekly sync and negotiated batch export after learning SLA constraints
Outcome: launched two weeks late but clean

Follow-up: What did you do next? - set up sync and mapped latency requirements
senior.raiseFeedback: The candidate initially underestimated cross-org dependencies. After the follow-up they describe building a regular sync and adjusting scope based on the other team's constraints. This raises the bar for senior because the story shows influence without authority and a measurable trade-off on timeline to protect quality.

lowerTranscript.text: I needed data from the risk team for a fraud feature. Their API wasn't documented well so I reverse-engineered it.
What did you miss at first?
Their data was delayed by a day. I found out after we started testing.
Not really, I just added a cache layer on our side to mask the delay.

senior.lowerFeedback: The candidate worked around the other team rather than understanding their constraints. The cache solution hid the problem instead of resolving it. For a senior this lowers the bar because there is no evidence of cross-team influence or sustainable delivery.

raiseTranscript.text: We were rolling out a new subscription tier. Finance needed a different revenue recognition model that required changes to our billing ledger.
What did you miss at first?
I assumed the ledger change was a one-quarter project. Finance walked me through ASC 606 implications and the audit trail requirements that would affect two future quarters.
How did you adjust the plan?

I reprioritized the billing roadmap, added a finance liaison to the steering committee, and delayed the tier launch by one quarter to avoid restatement risk. The change reduced audit findings by 40 percent the following year.
